23.16.42.en: In Him I am filled with hope, but in a spirit of reverence and godliness!

23.16.43.en: In Him I remember the day of Your coming, and cry out:

23.16.44.en: My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready!

23.16.45.en: Come, O Lord Jesus, for You are the Judge, and You are the Comforter and the Intercessor for me.

24.0.s.en: 1. The indifference of the wicked toward the Judge

24.0.0.en: Why, seeing times are not hidden from the Almighty, do they that know him not see his days? [1]

24.0.1.en: As Job looks toward the day of judgment, he is filled with awe, or the fear of the Lord, for there he meets the One who is above time (Job 15:17-23). Job is amazed at the wicked, that although they are subject to time, living for a while and then departing, they do not fear God, who embraces all times and from whom no time escapes. Job sees that every man appears at a certain time and then disappears by his death, and does not know the day of the Lord's coming to judge him. It would therefore have been fitting for him not to practice injustice against his brother; perhaps by this he turns the accusation directed against him toward his friends, who do not fear God and do not care about their friend Job, but practice cruelty against him.

24.0.2.en: The times are not hidden from the Almighty. Past times are not hidden from His judgment (Eccl 3:15), present times are not hidden from the ordering of His providence (Mt 10:29), and future times are not hidden from His foreknowledge (Acts 15:18). Therefore it is fitting that the wicked should not think they escape the divine justice, since the past, like the present and the future, is before the presence of God. They have no right to say: "The LORD seeth us not; the LORD hath forsaken the earth" (Ezek 8:12; 9:9). The wicked have no right to say that wicked men lived in the past and spent all their lives in ease, prosperity and success, for even if they died, they will rise to be judged before the Judge from whom nothing is hidden. The Lord has hidden the day of His coming from men so that all may cease from their evils, lest He come upon them suddenly. The general day of judgment is called the day of the Lord (Ps 37:13); it is surely coming, but we do not know it.

24.0.3.en: * "The times are not hidden from the Almighty" [1]... We are hidden within the divisions of time, since we are created beings. But God, the Creator of all things, embraces our times... And concerning eternity, we have such thoughts as these: we do not yet know the appointed time of eternity.

24.0.5.en: Since we do not know the day of the Lord's coming for judgment, while all times are open before Him, the discipline of earnestly awaiting the Lord's coming, with a person examining himself daily in a spirit of hope in Christ, the Savior of sinners, and in the work of the Holy Spirit, was vital in the early Church, especially in monastic communities.

24.0.6.en: * Every one must draw out from himself each day the story of his deeds by night and by day. If he has sinned, let him cease from sin; if he has not sinned, he must not boast, but hold fast to what is good without neglect, and not judge his brethren or justify himself [until the Lord comes, who reveals the hidden things] (1 Cor 4:5; Rom 2:16), as the blessed Apostle Paul says. For often we have unwittingly done things that we do not know, but the Lord sees everything. Therefore, since we commit the judgment to Him, let us be kind to one another, let us bear one another's burdens (Gal 6:2), but let us examine ourselves and hasten to fill up what is lacking in us.

24.0.7.en: * My son, do not rebuke anyone quickly, for this is a fall for you. Rather, remember your departure from this body at all times, and do not forget the eternal judgment, for if you do so you will not sin again. For our spiritual fathers said: solitude is the study (that is, the meditation) in the remembrance of death and the flight from all the things of the body.

24.1.s.en: 2. Their work of plunder and seizure

24.1.1.en: They violently take away flocks, and feed thereof [2].

24.1.2.en: Job looks at those around him and sees them indifferent to the just Judge. They remove the landmarks, that is, they seize the fields and lands of others, placing the boundaries of their own land (their landmarks) inside the land of another, and they seize their sheep and shepherd them as though they were theirs by right.

24.1.3.en: Here he begins with the first and gravest kind of evils, those which the Holy One cannot bear, namely the practice of injustice.

24.1.4.en: Nothing grieves the heart of God like injustice taking the place of love and truth. Man was created to be an icon of love, but [I saw under the sun... in the place of truth, there was injustice] (Eccl 3:16). There is none who cares for the tears of the oppressed, while their oppressors are arrogant (Eccl 4:1).

24.1.5.en: This practice was forbidden (Deut 19:14), and whoever violates the Law deserves the curse (Deut 27:17). As for seizing the flock, the prophet David judged the man who slaughtered the poor man's ewe lamb to be worthy of death (2 Sam 12:4-5), not realizing that he was judging himself, since he had seized the wife of Uriah the Hittite.

24.1.6.en: * "O Lord, why do the wicked flee from their hour, transgress the boundaries, and carry off the flock together with the shepherd?" Once more there is doubt, and he asks: Why do the wicked prosper...? Just as we do not know why one man falls under such sufferings unjustly while another brings them upon him, so naturally these injustices cause disturbance and affect one party as well as the other (the unjust and the wronged).

24.2.0.en: "They go forth like wild asses in a field" [6], meaning that they have despised the whole world, since they treat everyone lightly, thinking that there is no one who wrongs them and no one who does evil to them.

24.2.1.en: "But He (God) has not yet visited them." He will do so later, but He will scrutinize their faults and will not let them pass!

24.2.2.en: St. John Chrysostom says: The Preacher (Solomon the Wise) says: "And moreover I saw under the sun the place of truth, that injustice was there; and the place of justice, that wrong was there. I said in mine heart, God shall judge the righteous and the wicked: for there is a time there for every purpose and for every work" (Eccl 3:16-17). For the good God has made everything beautiful in its time, and the corruption that has come upon the world is not from the nature of the world itself, but through man's injustice and wrong toward his fellow man. And what testimony to the vanity of the world is like injustice occupying the place of truth, and wrong the place of justice? Corruption spreads into the depths of the courts of justice! But the Preacher believes in the just judgment of God. The corruption of the world does not mean that things proceed in a random manner without restraint; rather, God awaits the proper time to judge the righteous and the wicked. "For there is a time there for every purpose and for every work." In other words, if man by his corruption has wronged the world, since he has not put everything in its proper time and place, so that injustice has taken the place of justice... God intervenes to set the situation right, but also in His own time.

24.2.3.en: Perhaps among the gravest vices which the Holy Bible attacks, in both Testaments, is man's injustice toward his brother.

24.2.4.en: In His longsuffering God awaits our return to Him, that we may practice His love and righteousness; but the wicked insist on practicing violence and injustice. On the day of judgment, it seems as though God does not point out the details of their evils, but calls all their evils injustice, as if there were nothing that grieves the heart of God like man's injustice toward his fellow man. He addresses the wicked, saying: "I tell you, I know you not whence ye are; depart from me, all ye workers of injustice" (Lk 13:27). "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear! even cry out unto thee of injustice, and thou wilt not save!" (Hab 1:2).

24.2.5.en: The Holy Bible warns us against a man practicing injustice against his brother, affirming the gravity of injustice:

24.2.6.en: A. There is no refuge from injustice other than taking refuge in God Himself.

24.2.7.en: "Deliver me, O LORD, from the evil man; preserve me from the man of injustice" (Ps 140:1).

24.2.8.en: "Keep me, O LORD, from the hands of the wicked; preserve me from the man of injustice; who have purposed to overthrow my goings" (Ps 140:4).

24.2.9.en: B. The injustice that a man practices he only stores up for himself, and the injustice returns upon him to his destruction; he drinks from the very cup that he filled for his brother.

24.2.10.en: "Let not an evil speaker be established in the earth: evil shall hunt the man of injustice to his destruction" (Ps 140:11).

24.2.11.en: C. Injustice makes man lose wisdom and prudence, so that folly rules over him, and it deprives him of entering into a covenant with God, who is altogether just. For there is no fellowship between injustice and justice.

24.2.12.en: "Surely oppression maketh a wise man mad; and a gift destroyeth the heart" (Eccl 7:7).

24.2.13.en: "Wherefore thus saith the Holy One of Israel, Because ye despise this word, and trust in oppression and perverseness, and stay thereon" (Isa 30:12).

24.2.14.en: "For I the LORD love justice, I hate robbery by injustice; and I will make their reward faithful, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them" (Isa 61:8).

24.2.15.en: D. Injustice corrupts the spirit of shepherding, and makes leaders and rulers lose their pastoral work.

24.2.16.en: "Thus saith the Lord GOD; Let it suffice you, O princes of Israel: remove violence and robbery, and execute justice and righteousness, take away injustice from my people" (Ezek 45:9).

24.2.17.en: E. Every injustice enters, as into the storehouses of the palaces of those who think they are great and above the law, and there it settles; it will not go out without repentance and returning to You.

24.2.18.en: "For they know not to do right, saith the LORD, who store up injustice and robbery in their palaces" (Amos 3:10).

24.2.19.en: "Ye that put far away the evil day, and cause the seat of injustice to come near" (Amos 6:3).

24.2.20.en: "But let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and cry mightily unto God: yea, let them turn every one from his evil way, and from the injustice that is in their hands" (Jon 3:8).

24.2.21.en: F. Injustice corrupts the heart, the city of God Jerusalem, and the inner temple.

24.2.22.en: "They build up Zion with blood, and Jerusalem with injustice" (Mic 3:10).

24.2.23.en: "For he hateth divorce, saith the LORD, the God of Israel, and that one cover injustice with his garment, saith the LORD of hosts: therefore take heed to your spirit, that ye deal not treacherously" (Mal 2:16).

24.2.24.en: The psalmist sets the word "injustice" as though it were equal to the devil himself, placing injustice over against God, the object of our trust and our hope, and he warns us: "Trust not in injustice," as though there were before us one of two choices: God or injustice.

24.2.25.en: * "Trust not in injustice" (Ps 62:10). For my hope is in God... I have leapt up and placed my hope in God; can there be, in any way, injustice in God?

24.2.26.en: St. Augustine G. The outcome of injustice is vanity; it has no value.

24.2.27.en: "Trust not in injustice, and become not vain in robbery: if riches increase, set not your heart upon them" (Ps 62:10).

24.2.28.en: God has not promised His believers to remove injustice and persecutions from them, but He permits this for their glory and for His own glory in them, as a Savior who turns evils into good.

24.2.29.en: The psalmist says: "He shall redeem their soul from injustice and robbery: and precious shall their blood be in his sight" (Ps 72:14). Or, as it appears in some translations: "His name shall be honored in their presence."

24.2.30.en: * If Christians appear despised in this world, their name is honored in the presence of God. He no longer remembers the names with which they were formerly associated (and the labors) through Gentile (pagan) trifles, nor does He refer to the names that attached to them through their evil conduct before they became Christians. For they have received the name of Christians in the presence of God, the name that appears despised among their enemies.

24.2.31.en: St. Augustine In St. Augustine's commentary on Psalm 140, where the psalmist prays that God would keep him from the man of injustice, he sees that the psalmist gives us a living example of prayer against the unjust, in saying: "From the man of injustice deliver me... The proud have hid a snare for me, and cords; they have spread a net by the wayside; they have set gins for me" (Ps 140:4-5). For the prayer is not against the unjust man himself, but against evil and injustice, that God may remove the nets set against us.

24.2.32.en: * Many pray unskillfully against the wicked... It is fitting for you to pray against such nets, lest you lose your heavenly inheritance, lest you lose Christ, with whom you have a share in the inheritance; it has been appointed for you to live with Him forever, He who has made you an heir. For you have become an heir not by means of one whom you succeed after his death (the father according to the flesh), but by means of Him who lives with him forever.

24.2.33.en: St. Augustine True injustice, in the mind of St. Augustine, is not that which causes you material or temporal losses, such as seizing your inheritance or your possessions, but rather the setting of a snare for the soul so that it is deprived of fellowship with the Lord Christ in the eternal inheritance.

24.2.34.en: When the unjust man sets nets to catch the righteous, they themselves fall into their own snares and destroy their eternity. As the psalmist says: "Evil shall hunt the man of injustice to his destruction" (Ps 140:11).

24.2.35.en: * Evils come, but the wicked man does not endure; therefore he says: [it hunts him to his destruction]. For many of the good and righteous have been struck by evils, yet through the evils they were found (and did not perish). When evils pursued the good, that is, our martyrs, and seized them, they hunted them, but not to destruction. Their bodies were pressed, but the spirit was crowned. The spirit was taken from the body, but nothing befalls the body, which is hidden away for the future.

24.2.36.en: Let the body be burned and scourged and disfigured; is it taken away from its Creator because it was delivered into the hand of its persecutors? Will not He who created it out of nothing restore it in a better form than it had?

24.2.37.en: St. Augustine Pope Gregory (the Great) sees in Job's friends, who symbolize the heretics, that they constantly use every means, whether by enticement or deceit, to enlarge their borders and to plunder souls, by removing the marks that the Fathers set, that is, the evangelical, ecclesial and patristic concepts, so that they draw some away and turn them aside from the divine field. They take the gentle flock of Christ and count it as their own flock, and claim the right to shepherd this flock outside the Church of Christ.

24.2.38.en: * "Others remove the landmarks, and violently take away flocks and feed them" [2]. Whom does he indicate under the title "others" but the heretics, since they are strangers to the bosom of the holy Church? They remove the landmarks in order to overstep the ordinances of the Fathers by walking in a crooked way. Concerning these ordinances it is written: [Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set] (Prov 28:22).

24.3.0.en: They drive away the ass of the fatherless, they take the widow's ox for a pledge [3].

24.3.1.en: He gives another example of injustice, which is that a man seizes the donkey of a poor orphan to profit from it materially, and the poor man cannot contend with the one who seized it. Or one who takes as a pledge the ox of a widow who uses it in her small field, for one reason or another, such as in payment of a small debt or of overdue rent. The wicked do not cease taking what is not theirs, so they covet the use of the orphans' donkey and take the widow's ox as a pledge.

24.3.2.en: God regards the injustice that falls upon an orphan or a widow as directed to Himself personally, for He is "a father of the fatherless, and a judge of the widows" (Ps 68:5); "He doth execute the judgment of the fatherless and widow, and loveth the stranger, in giving him food and raiment" (Deut 10:18). "The LORD preserveth the strangers; he relieveth the fatherless and widow: but the way of the wicked he maketh crooked" (Ps 146:9). "He will not despise the supplication of the fatherless; nor the widow, if she pour out her complaint" (Sir 35:17). God has laid down many commandments concerning care for the orphan and the widow, of which we mention the following:

24.3.3.en: "Thou shalt not pervert the judgment of the stranger, nor of the fatherless; nor take a widow's raiment to pledge" (Deut 24:17).

24.3.4.en: "When thou cuttest down thine harvest in thy field, and hast forgot a sheaf in the field, thou shalt not go again to fetch it: it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow: that the LORD thy God may bless thee in all the work of thine hands" (Deut 24:19).

24.3.5.en: "When thou beatest thine olive tree, thou shalt not go over the boughs again: it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow" (Deut 24:20).

24.3.6.en: "When thou gatherest the grapes of thy vineyard, thou shalt not glean it afterward: it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow" (Deut 24:21).

24.3.7.en: "When thou hast made an end of tithing all the tithes of thine increase the third year, which is the year of tithing, and hast given it unto the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow, that they may eat within thy gates, and be filled" (Deut 26:12).

24.3.8.en: "Cursed be he that perverteth the judgment of the stranger, fatherless, and widow. And all the people shall say, Amen" (Deut 27:19).

24.3.9.en: "Thus saith the LORD; Execute ye judgment and righteousness, and deliver the spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor: and the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow, do not oppress, nor wrong, neither shed innocent blood in this place" (Jer 22:3).

24.3.10.en: "And oppress not the widow, nor the fatherless, the stranger, nor the poor; and let none of you imagine evil against his brother in your heart" (Zech 7:10).

24.3.11.en: "And I will come near to you to judgment; and I will be a swift witness against the sorcerers, and against the adulterers, and against false swearers, and against those that oppress the hireling in his wages, the widow and the fatherless, and that turn aside the stranger from his right, and fear not me, saith the LORD of hosts" (Mal 3:5).

24.3.12.en: * Flee also, O bishop, from him who oppresses the widow, and from him who is strong against the orphan, and from him who is also cruel to his servants with blows or famine or evil dominion; their offerings are hated, and you are not to accept them.

24.3.13.en: The Didascalia * Priests ought to be compassionate and merciful toward all, bringing back those who have strayed, visiting the sick, and not neglecting the widow, the orphan and the poor, but always [taking care of good things before the Lord and men] (cf. Rom 12:17; 2 Cor 8:21), refraining from all anger, from partiality toward men, and from issuing an unjust judgment, fleeing from every love of money, not hasty in judging against anyone, not harsh in judgment, knowing that we are all debtors through sin.

24.3.14.en: Polycarp, Bishop of Smyrna * Your ministry will shine with greater brilliance if you resist the distress that befalls the widow and the poor at the hands of a man in authority, with the help of the Church, showing that the commandment of the Lord carries greater weight with you than courtesy to the rich.

24.3.15.en: St. Ambrose Perhaps among the most important forms of injustice that the Fathers of the early Church took care to warn the people against is usury, and the exploitation of their poor brothers by the rich, who lend to them at interest that causes them countless troubles. We have already spoken about usury in our book "Social Thought among the Fathers of the Church."

24.3.16.en: St. John Chrysostom presents to us a bitter picture of the rich exploiting poor families, lending to them at exorbitant interest that destroys these families.

24.3.17.en: * When a family becomes poor, it is driven to borrow in order to survive. But if the creditor demands interest on the debt, then this family falls even deeper into the pit. It is obliged not only to repay the debt but also the interest that accumulates on it. The creditor may claim, even to himself, that he is acting with propriety, but in fact he is acting with great cunning behind the appearance of giving, deliberately harming another.

24.3.18.en: He trades at the expense of the misfortunes of others, and profits from their calamity.

24.3.19.en: He seeks to gain material things under the guise of an act of mercy, and thus turns giving into theft. He appears to moor the poor family in a harbor of safety, but in truth he drives the ship toward the rocks. The creditor may ask: Why must I lend money to others when it is useful to me, and not ask for a reward for it? And the answer is that you will receive a reward: in return for the gold you lent on earth, you will receive gold in heaven at a rate of interest far greater than you can imagine.

24.3.20.en: St. John Chrysostom If we take the symbolic interpretation, the donkey of the orphan which the wicked heretics use signifies the plundering of simple souls from the bosom of the Church and their exploitation, as they bind them with the burden of the error of their faith and their beliefs. He calls him an orphan because he has not realized his sonship to God his Father and to the Church his mother, so he is an orphan of father and mother, and does not enjoy the peace of God and the joy of the Church his mother. The taking of the widow's ox as a pledge signifies the soul that does not perceive the Church as a joyful bride, and so walks in great sorrow like a widow. Such souls the heretics seize with temporary enticements, while they rob them even of their one ox, so that they are inwardly in want and need!

24.3.21.en: * "They drive away the ass of the fatherless, and take the widow's ox for a pledge" [3]... The ass is used to carry people's burdens. So he is like a kind of ass among the elect, submitting himself to bear earthly matters, bearing burdens for the benefit of men. Often when heretics seduce such a person and draw him away from the bosom of the Church, he is like one whose orphan's ass has been driven away, for they bind him to accept the error of their faith. They draw him away from his inclination toward what is good.

24.3.22.en: What is understood by the "widow" but the holy Church, which is deprived, for a time, of seeing her slain Bridegroom? Now the ox of this widow is each preacher individually. Rightly he adds here "for a pledge," for when the pledge is taken away, something truly remains in our hands while the other is sought.

24.4.0.en: They turn the needy out of the way.

24.4.1.en: The poor of the earth hide themselves together [4].

24.4.2.en: The injustice of the wicked does not stop at seizing the possessions of others, lands and fields and flocks, and exploiting the little that the needy and the destitute have; rather, they think that the world was created for them, and that the poor have no right to live. So they spend all their effort to remove them from the earth, until the poor are compelled to flee and hide from their faces.

24.4.3.en: The unjust find their pleasure when they block the ways of escape before the poor, and threaten them that they will take vengeance on them as vagabonds; and when the poor hide in order to slip out of their hands, they mock them.

24.4.4.en: * "They turn the needy out of the way, and the meek of the earth are pressed together" [4]. Humility is often indicated by the expression "need" (poverty), and very many who appear meek and humble, if they do not hold fast to discernment, fall by imitating others.

24.4.6.en: God Himself inclines His ears to hear the sighs of the simple and the meek whom no one cares about. The psalmist says: "LORD, thou hast heard the groaning of the meek; thou wilt establish their heart, thou wilt incline thine ear to do justice for the fatherless and the crushed, that the man of the earth may no more terrify them" (Ps 10:17-18).

24.4.7.en: * "His eyes watch the poor" (Ps 10:8), for he persecutes in particular the righteous, of whom it is said: [Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven](a), [He lieth in wait secretly as a lion in his den] (Ps 10:9). By the lion in a pit he means a violent man whose work is deceit... He draws him to himself by violence, with every torment that he can bring upon him... "LORD, thou hast heard the groaning of the meek" (Ps 10:17), this groaning that comes forth while they are burning, since, in the afflictions and troubles of this world, they long for the coming of the day of the Lord... [to do justice for the fatherless and the crushed, that he may no more terrify them] (Ps 10:18), and not for the sake of those who are conformed to the world nor for the proud.

24.5.s.en: 5. They think they are above the law

24.5.0.en: Behold, as wild asses in the wilderness, they go forth to their work; they rise early for food.

24.5.1.en: The wilderness yieldeth bread for them and for their children [5].

24.5.2.en: Job likens the wicked to the wild asses that range in the wilderness with no law to govern them. They rise early in the morning to eat, and look to the wilderness to provide food for their young. So the wicked count themselves above the law, with no work except eating and drinking and pleasures, and providing every pleasure for their children.

24.5.3.en: "In the wilderness": the wicked wish that the whole earth would be turned into wilderness, where there is no room for laws that govern society, and so injustice can be practiced on a wider scale. The wilderness is the most suitable place for savage people like these; yet there is no wilderness that hides a man from God or places him beyond His reach.

24.5.4.en: "They go forth to their work," which is robbery, for they have made plunder and the practice of injustice their constant occupation, from which they gain great profits. In their eyes they practice this profession with energy and zeal, for they "rise early for food" with prey. They go forth as to their work, as a man goeth forth unto his work (Ps 104:23), and as the righteous rise early to the Lord and glorify Him, the wicked go forth to the practice of injustice as a task to which they are committed. Thus the wicked rise early to practice their work. They spend the night planning evil, and when the morning dawns they hasten to carry out in practice what is in their hearts. As it was said of Ephraim: "He is like the Canaanite, the balances of deceit are in his hand: he loveth to oppress. And Ephraim said, Yet I am become rich, I have found me out wealth" (Hos 12:7-8).

24.5.5.en: "The wilderness yieldeth bread for them and for their children," for they provide for themselves and for their children from the plunder that they practice on the roads of the wilderness, instead of providing by honorable means.

24.5.6.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the heretics behave in this way, since they live in a barren wilderness, where they leave the Church, the house of God and His holy vineyard. They are unrestrained; what occupies them is pleasures and temporal goods, and they do not want any restraint or submission to any ordering such as fasting, prayer, prostrations (metanoias), etc., and if divine discipline comes upon them they do not care. Thus they live in a barren wilderness without fruit of the Spirit. They resemble Ishmael, of whom it was said: he will be a wild man; his hand will be against every man, and every man's hand against him (Gen 16:11-12).

24.5.7.en: * "Others, like wild asses (onagers) in the wilderness, go forth to their work" [5]. For the onager is a wild ass. Here the heretics are rightly likened to wild asses, since they are unrestrained in their pleasures and are strangers to the bonds of faith and sober-mindedness. Therefore it is written: [A wild ass used to the wilderness, that snuffeth up the wind at her pleasure] (Jer 24:2). A person is a wild ass used to the wilderness when he does not till the soil of his heart with the loftiness of discipline, and so dwells where there is no fruit... This is not the work of God, but their own work, that they do not follow sound teachings but follow their lusts. For it is written: [He that walketh in a perfect way, he shall serve me] (Ps 6:101).

24.5.9.en: * I know that what I am saying is painful, but how much benefit it contains! If the rich man had found someone to give him such advice, instead of flattering him and saying what he wanted to hear and drawing him into sliding into a life of extravagance, he would not have fallen into that abyss. He would not have come under that unbearable torment, repenting too late, seeking comfort; but everyone was working to give him pleasure, handing him over to the hell of fire.

24.5.10.en: I wish that we would preach and speak always and continually on this subject, for the Holy Bible says: "In all thy works remember thy latter end, and thou shalt never do amiss" (Sir 7:40), and likewise it says: [Prepare your work for your departure, and make everything ready for the road] (cf. Prov 24:27).

24.5.11.en: St. John Chrysostom * However green the wicked may be, they will perish, for they have been kept for the fire... These flourish in the happiness of the world, and perish by the power of God. They do not perish in the same way as they flourish; they flourish for a time, and perish eternally. They flourish in what is not truly good, and perish in real torments.

24.5.12.en: St. Augustine The psalmist was looking at the wicked living in peace in this world and in prosperity, like those who are in happiness, and he envied them and was jealous of them; therefore he confessed, saying: "But as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped. For I was envious at the proud (sinners), when I saw the prosperity of the wicked. For there are no bands in their death, and their body is fat. They are not in trouble as other men; neither are they plagued with other men. Therefore pride compasseth them about as a chain; they put on their injustice as a garment" (Ps 73:2-6).

24.5.13.en: * I observed the sinners and saw them in peace. What peace? A temporal, temporary, earthly and fallen peace, and yet this (peace) I ask from God. I saw that those who do not serve God have what I desired in order that I might serve God, so my feet slipped, and my steps slipped. But why do the wicked have this...? They cannot avoid their death, and their punishment is perpetual... Now I knew why they have peace and prosper on the earth. For death surely awaits them eternally; they do not avoid these things and will not be able to be saved from them... for their punishment will not be temporary but fixed and eternal.

24.6.s.en: 6. They want evil, and the Lord wants good

24.6.0.en: 6 They reap their fodder in the field, and they glean the vineyard of the wicked. 7 They cause the naked to lodge without clothing, that they have no covering in the cold. 8 They are wet with the showers of the mountains, and embrace the rock for want of a shelter. 9 "They pluck the fatherless from the breast, and take a pledge of the poor. 10 They cause him to go naked without clothing, and being hungry they carry the sheaves. 11 They make oil within their walls, and tread their winepresses, and suffer thirst.

24.6.1.en: They reap their fodder in the field, and they glean the vineyard of the wicked [6].

24.6.2.en: Since they feel that they are above the law, they reap the fields of others and offer their produce as fodder for their animals. It is as though they count their animals better than the owners of the fields, so they do not care about the hunger of the owners of the seized fields, even though the produce is offered not to men but to animals.

24.6.3.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that the field here and the vineyard refer to the Holy Bible. For the heretics pick passages from it and distort their meanings in service of their own passions.

24.6.4.en: * "They reap a field that is not theirs, and they gather by violence the vineyard of him whom they oppress" [6]. The field refers to the wide realm of Holy Scripture, which the heretics reap as though it were not theirs, for they pick from it passages to bear meanings quite far from what they mean. This is also described by the title "vineyard," which offers clusters of virtues through the words of truth. They are like those who press upon the owner of the vineyard, the author of Holy Scripture, with violence, for they distort by violence the meanings of the words of Holy Scripture. As (the Lord) said: [Thou hast made me to serve with thy sins, thou hast wearied me with thine iniquities] (Isa 24:43). And they gather the wine of that vineyard, for they gather together clusters of passages from it after turning them aside to their own notions.

24.6.5.en: The field or the vineyard can also be understood as the universal Church, which the corrupt preachers reap, and they press upon her Creator in His members, "gathering the wine together," by gaining control of persons who seem to be righteous.

24.6.7.en: Origen believes that the heretics first receive the deposit of faith, and later turn aside from it. [Heretics begin with faith, and then later turn aside from the way of faith and from the truth of the Church's teaching.] In their pride, the heretics search the divine Scripture not to discover the truth, but to confirm their own doctrines. Henri de Lubac says in his book on Origen:

24.6.8.en: [One must receive the faith in God in the Spirit in which the Church teaches us, and not behave like the heretics who search the Scripture merely to find what confirms their own doctrines. Their pride lifts them "higher than the cedars of Lebanon." Their sophistry is full of deceit. It is of no use for them to claim that they have a tradition descending to them from the Apostles, for they are masters of error.

24.6.9.en: While the faithful Christian never strays from the great tradition, in order to confirm their lies they wish to make us worship a "Christ" whom they have invented in a "wilderness," whereas our true Christ reveals Himself "inside the house." They distort those vessels of gold and silver, which are the holy texts, in order to fashion them in accordance with their passions. They are thieves and fornicators, who lay hands on the divine words with one purpose, namely to distort them with their perverse interpretations. They are counterfeiters, for they have coined their doctrines outside the Church. False teachers and false prophets, they spin out of the daughters of their own thoughts what they propose. They are the liars of whom Ezekiel spoke, who by their deceitful trickery daub their idols, which are their hollow doctrines, with sweetness for the one who listens to them, to make their deviation more certain. All of them claim that Jesus is their teacher and embrace Him. But their kiss is the kiss of Judas.]

24.6.10.en: They cause the naked to lodge without clothing, that they have no covering in the cold [7].

24.6.11.en: Again, since they are subject to no law, they strip others of their clothes and drive them out, so these spend the night without coverings to protect them from the bitter cold.

24.6.12.en: Thus the heretics spend all their effort to strip the believers of their garments, that is, the true fellowship with the Lord Christ, of whom the Apostle Paul says: "Ye have put on Christ" (Gal 3:27), "and have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him" (Col 3:10). He also says:

24.6.13.en: "And that ye put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness" (Eph 4:24).

24.6.14.en: "Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil" (Eph 6:11).

24.6.15.en: "Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering" (Col 3:12).

24.6.16.en: "And above all these things put on love, which is the bond of perfectness" (Col 3:14).

24.6.17.en: * "They drive out the naked, and take their garments, those who have no covering in the cold" [7]. As garments cover the body, so good works do for the soul. Therefore it was said: [Blessed is he that watcheth, and keepeth his garments, lest he walk naked, and they see his shame] (Rev 15:16). When the heretics shatter the good works in someone's mind, they clearly strip off his garments. It was well said: "They have no covering in the cold," for the covering is related to righteousness, and the cold to sin.

24.6.19.en: * "Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" (1 Cor 8:5).

24.6.20.en: And as we put off the old man and his deeds, we put on the new man, created after God (Eph 22:4, 24), and meditate in the law of God day and night, with a humble mind and a pure conscience.

24.6.21.en: Let us cast off from us all hypocrisy and deceit, keeping far from all hypocrisy and cunning.

24.6.22.en: May we pledge ourselves to the love of God and love of neighbor, that we may become a new creation, partaking of new wine...

24.6.23.en: Therefore let us keep the feast as we ought.

24.6.24.en: * We need to put on the Lord Jesus in order that we may be able to celebrate the feast with Him. Now we put Him on when we love virtue and are enemies of evil... when we love righteousness and not injustice, and honor contentment and have strength of mind, and do not forget the poor but open our doors to all men, and do not forget humility of mind and hate pride.

24.6.25.en: Pope Abba Athanasius the Apostolic * If the garment of your soul is "covetousness," put on another instead of it, and come, take off your old garment and do not put it on again.

24.6.26.en: I beg you to take off fornication and uncleanness, and to put on the shining garment of purity.

24.6.27.en: I command you this before the Bridegroom Jesus enters and looks at your garment.

24.6.28.en: I leave you a long time for repentance. It is an ample opportunity for you to take off, wash, put on, and enter!

24.6.29.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem They are wet with the showers of the mountains, and embrace the rock for want of a shelter [8].

24.6.30.en: As the wicked work to rob the believers of their faith in the Lord Christ, to deprive them of the divine garments and the heavenly covering, these poor people become naked, suffering from the rains of the mountains, where they have no shelter in which to take cover from the rain, and they look for stones to embrace, or some rock that might cover them from the rain.

24.6.31.en: * "They are wet with the rains of the mountains, and embrace the stones for want of a garment" [8]. The rains of the mountains are the words of the teachers. Of these same mountains it was said in the voice of the holy Church: [I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills] (Ps 1:121). These persons are drenched by the rains of the mountains, those who are filled to the end with the streams of the holy Fathers. And the garment that we receive as a covering is good conduct, with which a man is covered so that the filth of his corruption may be covered in the eyes of Almighty God. So it is written: [Blessed are they whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered] (Ps 1:32). Who are those whom we understand by the title "stones" but the strong ones within the borders of the holy Church, those to whom it is proclaimed by the Shepherd: [Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house] (1 Pet 2:5). So also those who, on the basis of their practical conduct, have no complacency in them, fly to the protection of the holy martyrs, and practice tears and supplications at their holy relics in order to obtain forgiveness through their intercession. What then are these doing by such abasement but embracing stones, since they lack the covering of good practice?

24.6.33.en: They pluck the fatherless from the breast, and take a pledge of the poor [9].

24.6.34.en: In their violence the wicked snatch the orphan while he is nursing at his mother's breasts, and seek out the poor to use them as pledges. They have no pity on the nursing infant that he is deprived of his mother, nor on the mother that she is deprived of her infant also. They choose a critical time, snatching the infant while he is nursing, and they care nothing for his cries and his hunger!

24.6.35.en: Pharaoh killed the children of the Hebrews, and so did Herod in order to kill the child King; these snatched the children and infants from their mothers' breasts with the sword.

24.6.36.en: Some think that the unjust, after they kill the fathers, snatch the infants in order to deprive them of their mothers. Others think that they snatch the infants as slaves, as happened in the days of Nehemiah (Neh 5:5).

24.6.37.en: * "They use violence in preying upon the fatherless, and ruin the common flock of the poor" [9]... The heretics use violence in preying upon the orphans, for they attack with violence the weak minds of the believers by words and deeds.

24.6.38.en: As for "the common flock of the poor," they are the uneducated multitudes, who, if they had received the wealth of true knowledge, would not have had the covering of their faith taken from them. For the original teachers are like a kind of nobles (senators) within the borders of the holy Church, multiplying knowledge in the heart and increasing the true wealth that is in them, whereas the heretics ruin the common flock of the poor, taking the covering of faith from the uneducated, making them naked through their poisonous preaching, while they are not able to do this with the educated.

24.6.40.en: They cause him to go naked without clothing, and being hungry they carry the sheaves [10].

24.6.41.en: * "They take away the ears of wheat from the naked, and from those who walk without covering, and from the hungry" [10]. He says "naked" and then repeats "those who walk without covering," for there is a difference between being naked and walking naked. Everyone who does neither what is good nor what is evil is naked and trifling. But he who does evil "walks naked," for since he lacks the covering of good practice, he walks in the way of evil.

24.6.42.en: But some know the evil of their misery, and hasten to be satisfied with the bread of righteousness, and hunger to receive the sayings of Holy Scripture. When these change in mind, the sayings of the Fathers, for the reform of their minds, become as though they carried ears of wheat from a good harvest. And so the heretics take the ears of wheat from the naked, and from those who walk without covering, and from the hungry.

24.6.44.en: They make oil within their walls.

24.6.45.en: They tread their winepresses, and suffer thirst [11].

24.6.46.en: The wicked do not cease from trampling upon the children of God in order to humiliate and crush them. But they do not know that as they tread upon them with their feet, the believers are turned into perfume, and into joyful spiritual wine.

24.6.47.en: What does he mean by saying: "within their walls"? The wicked wish to humiliate the believers and trample them inside the walls of the city, that is, they break into their places and insult them in their homes. But God turns the city into a holy winepress, that the believers may share in their crucified Christ, who says: [I have trodden the winepress alone] (Isa 63:3). The wicked tread the winepress, and the winepress overflows with wine that rejoices the heart of God and in which the heavenly ones take pride, while the wicked come out of the winepress in a state of thirst, obtaining nothing from their violence but emptiness.

24.6.48.en: * "They rest at midday among the heaps (threshing floors), thirsting for the winepress of trodden wine" [11]. All who persecute the holy Church, what do they do but tread the winepress? This is permitted through the divine dispensation, so that the clusters of the soul may overflow with spiritual wine, since they are stripped of the corruptible body, and so flow in the heavenly places as in a vessel. For while the wicked tread upon the righteous, they are like those who place clusters of grapes under their feet.

24.6.50.en: * The cluster does not become wine, nor the olive oil, unless the stone of the press passes over them.

24.6.51.en: * The soul does not return to God unless it is torn away from the world, and nothing truly tears it away but toil and pain.

24.7.s.en: 7. They think that God does not pay attention!

24.7.0.en: 12 From the pain men groan, and the soul of the wounded crieth out, yet God payeth no attention to injustice. 13 "They are among those that rebel against the light; they know not the ways thereof, nor abide in the paths thereof.

24.7.1.en: From the pain men groan, and the soul of the wounded crieth out, yet God payeth no attention to injustice [12].

24.7.2.en: Surely God hears the groans of the sufferers and the cry of the wounded, but since He turns the evil of the wicked into good for the sufferers, He seems like One who pays no attention to injustice. These are our feelings when injustice rules and wounds the believers, and we think that God is busy elsewhere than with His Church, and does not care about her wounds and the injustice that has fallen upon her! Perhaps Job means here that while the sufferers groan and the wounded cry out, the wicked mock them and go further in their evils, looking at God as if, in His heavens, He does not care about the injustice that falls upon men, whoever they may be!
